reefs.name: Great Barrier Reef
reefs.note: The world's largest reef system and a UNESCO World Heritage Site. It has suffered six mass bleaching events in under a decade, leaving little time for recovery between them.

reefs.name: Coral Triangle
reefs.where: Indonesia, Philippines, Malaysia, Papua New Guinea, Solomon Islands, Timor-Leste
reefs.note: The global centre of marine biodiversity, including Raja Ampat. Overfishing, blast fishing, coastal development and warming all put pressure on it.

reefs.name: Mesoamerican Reef
reefs.note: Stony coral tissue loss disease has spread through the region since 2018, and the 2023 marine heatwave caused severe bleaching across the Caribbean.

reefs.name: Florida's Coral Reef
reefs.note: Elkhorn and staghorn corals were listed as threatened under the US Endangered Species Act in 2006. The 2023 heatwave caused widespread bleaching and death, including in restoration nurseries.

reefs.name: Red Sea
reefs.where: Egypt, Saudi Arabia, Sudan, Eritrea, Israel, Jordan
reefs.note: Corals in the northern Red Sea tolerate unusually high temperatures, so scientists see the Gulf of Aqaba as a possible climate refuge. The south has bleached more often.

reefs.name: Persian Gulf
reefs.where: UAE, Qatar, Bahrain, Saudi Arabia, Iran
reefs.note: These corals survive the hottest seas of any reef, which makes them important for understanding heat tolerance. Large losses have still followed extreme summers.

reefs.name: Maldives
reefs.note: The whole nation is built on coral atolls, so reef health and the country's future are directly linked. Its reefs protect the islands from waves and rising seas.

reefs.name: Lakshadweep
reefs.note: India's only coral atolls. Repeated bleaching has reduced live coral cover, and the islands depend on these reefs for fishing and coastal protection.

reefs.name: Gulf of Mannar
reefs.note: Past coral mining and destructive fishing damaged these fringing reefs. Restoration and stricter protection have helped parts of the reef recover.

reefs.name: Andaman & Nicobar Islands
reefs.note: The richest coral reefs in India. The 2004 tsunami uplifted and damaged parts of the reef, and marine heatwaves have caused repeated bleaching since.

reefs.name: Ningaloo Reef
reefs.note: One of the world's largest fringing reefs, close enough to shore to swim to. It was relatively unharmed for many years but bleached during the 2025 heatwave.

reefs.name: New Caledonia
reefs.note: Its lagoons hold one of the most diverse reef systems in the world. Many reefs remain in comparatively good condition.

reefs.name: Sekisei Lagoon
reefs.note: Japan's Ministry of the Environment reported that about 70% of the lagoon's corals had died after the 2016 bleaching event.

reefs.name: Hawaiian Islands
reefs.note: Hawaiian reefs are isolated, so many of their species exist nowhere else. Back-to-back bleaching in 2014 and 2015 killed large areas of coral, especially in West Hawai‘i.

reefs.name: Chagos Archipelago
reefs.note: With almost no local pollution or fishing, these reefs show how coral recovers when heat is the only threat. They recovered after 1998 but bleached again in 2015 and 2016.

reefs.name: East African Coast
facts: Most of W. Indian Ocean reefs
reefs.note: The 1998 El Niño killed a large share of corals across the Western Indian Ocean. Many coastal communities depend directly on reef fisheries.

actions.title: Cut carbon emissions
actions.text: Ocean warming is the main driver of mass bleaching. Every fraction of a degree avoided keeps more reefs alive.

actions.title: Dive and snorkel with care
actions.text: Never touch, stand on or break coral. Use mineral sunscreen and keep fins clear of the reef.

actions.title: Never buy coral products
actions.text: In India, all reef-building corals are protected under Schedule I of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972.

actions.title: Support marine protected areas
actions.text: Well-managed protected areas reduce fishing and pollution pressure, which helps reefs recover between heatwaves.

actions.title: Report what you see
actions.text: Citizen-science programmes such as CoralWatch and Reef Check use photographs from the public to track bleaching.
